candidates.title: Capture the Milky Way Perfectly with THESE Tips!
candidates.description: Photographing the Milky Way might seem difficult, but with a few pointers and a simple guide, even novice shooters can capture amazing images of the galaxy. For starters, you need to find dark skies away from city lights. Go out on a night with little to no moon during the summer months to best capture the core of the Milky Way. Then, grab your tripod, DSLR or mirrorless camera, fast ultra-wide lens, and your headlamp. Dial your shutter speed to 20 seconds, your aperture to f2.8 (wider if you can), and ISO to 6400. Use manual focus, and press the shutter! It’s really that simple. If you want to capture amazing images of the night sky, make sure to save this video and send it to a friend who you want to capture the Milky Way with! Austin Jackson is a landscape and outdoor photographer based in Southern Utah. He loves capturing great light in some of the world’s most stunning locations. In addition to capturing his own images, Austin enjoys the content creation side of things, creating countless videos to help outdoor photographers improve their craft. Take our quiz to find what tiny is right for you - Interested In Being Featured On The Channel? : VIDEO DESCRIPTION: Diana has been a van person since college. At 60, she built her dream: a $170,000 2024 Noovo Lite with no propane, 40 gallons of water, and room for her, her dogs, and months of adventure at a time. Diana funded this build from her late mother's RV, a Sprinter-based C-class with plenty of equity. That sale closed the loop on 40 years of van life, from a college pop top to an Airstream, an A-class, a C-class, and now back to the van, exactly the way she always wanted it. The kitchen sits at the side door so steam and grease escape outside. Diana cooks fresh food on the road, and the induction cooktop, microwave, and 12-volt upright fridge with internal freezer all run off electric. Zero propane in this van. A pull-out pantry for dry goods and spices folds flush against the wall when she is done cooking. The dining area opens fully from the door with no walls cutting the sightline. Diana is a little claustrophobic, and this layout was a deciding factor. Light and bright, windows on all sides, table extension for prep, and room for three adults. The van does not feel small. candidates.description: When the Mary Rose sank in 1545 it was fully equipped for war and amongst the armaments were some massive finned incendiary darts. From composition and mise-en-scène to blocking within a fixed frame, we explore how filmmakers create tension, emotion, and visual clarity without moving the camera. You’ll learn: • What defines a static (locked-off) shot • The difference between static shots and camera movement • How to use blocking to create visual dynamism • How framing and composition carry meaning • When to choose a static shot over a moving camera • How editing affects static scenes Static cinematography isn’t about doing less — it’s about doing more within the frame. candidates.title: The Sketchiest Project I Ever Attempted. (No Water or Sewer for 4 Days)
candidates.description: What started as a sewer backup turned into one of the sketchiest projects I've ever attempted. A plumber came, ran his camera, cleared the roots — and then pushed it a little further. That's when we found pressurized water spraying inside the sewer pipe. Turns out I didn't just have a broken sewer line. I also had a busted main water line buried under my front yard. Right next to the foundation. So I did what any reasonable person would do. I rented a 3.5 ton excavator, took 4 days off work, and tried to replace both pipes myself. Nothing went according to plan. No water for days. My wife slowly losing patience. And me, 9 feet underground, questioning every decision I've ever made. This video is the full story — start to finish. The chaos, the mistakes, the moments where I genuinely thought I was in over my head (literally), and somehow, eventually, getting it done. If you enjoy watching someone try really hard and suffer a little bit along the way — welcome. candidates.title: Inside the Shenzhen Robot Factory That's Reinventing CNC
candidates.description: Thanks to NestWorks for sponsoring this video and showing us around! To learn more about the NestWorks C500 CNC mill and back their Kickstarter, go to: (affiliate link) Elephant Robotics in Shenzhen was spending over a million dollars a year on custom machined parts. But they couldn't find a CNC that met their needs, so they decided to build their own. I visited their offices and workshops, dug into the robots they’re building, and followed the story of how that pain led to a new kind of CNC they’re calling NestWorks. Let me show you how it works and why LiDAR may not ever come in a Tesla but matters for a robot mower. I test a lot of devices. Most of them, are frankly, kinda forgettable. Not that there’s anything wrong with them, they’re great. But they aren’t game-changers in my workflow or sports life. Instead, they are typically an iteration of an existing item I have. One watch for a newer watch. A new trainer for an older trainer. Or a slightly tweaked action cam replacing an older one. So when I first heard about the Oakley/Meta Vanguards, frankly, I figured it was going to be yet another smart glasses product that would end up in the bin of blah. I’ve tried countless ones over the years, from Recon Snow (2012+), Recon Jet (2013+), Google Glass (2014), Recon Jet (2013+), Garmin Varia Vision (2016), to the SOLOS glasses (2018), Everysight Raptor (2018), FORM Swim Goggles (2019+), and many more I never got around to writing about. And that ignores products like the Apple Vision Pro (2024), and making that work in sports too. When it came to the Oakley Meta Vanguard glasses, I was wrong. These are astoundingly good. They will absolutely replace a GoPro in a lot of cycling and even running action cam scenarios. But it’s more interesting to understand *why* and *how* they will do that. candidates.title: I Realistically Rebuilt Torino Into Italy's Best Club - Full Movie
candidates.description: Why Torino? They’re one of the absolute most interesting teams in the world. Torino were the innovators before innovation existed, one of the oldest teams in Italy, and were the dominant force either side of world war two. They were the first team to do the cup and league double in Italy, but this isn’t as interesting as the five consecutive titles they won in the 1940s. In 1947, every Italian national team outfielder played for Torino, with a goalkeeper from Juventus. They refused to play the classic Italian catenaccio, instead played fast flowing, high press football, well before that was popular. Their dominance ended in horrific circumstances in 1949. The plane that was carrying the clubs entire first team, reserves and coaching staff crashed approaching Turin. The club never recovered. They would win one more title in the 1970’s, but since 2013, they’ve never finished higher than 7th, or lower than 16th. History lesson over. We’re going to be managing Torino as realistically as we can, and over the next three episodes, take a mid table team, give them an identity, and try to bring back the era of Il Grande Torino. We’ll try to make a defensively strong side with believable transfers, we’ll let our best players go if the bids make sense, and be playing with in game events on high. candidates.title: This Tool Changer Took 2 YEARS To Build. Then This Happened.
candidates.description: My Sovol Tool Changer is FINALLY done-ish. Was it worth it? It's complicated. Brought to you by Sovol. Check out their new 7-toolheaded IDEX tool changer - the Sovol M1D: Two years ago, a few friends and I set out to build something money couldn't buy: a no-limits, 7 tool changer monster based on the Sovol SV08. Then, right as we were about to finish it, Sovol announced their own commercially available 7 tool changer 3d printer for just $1,400. So... was it worth it? From redesigns of the stealthchanger files and failed parts to Klipper firmware headaches and the occasional glimpse of success, this project has been equal parts engineering challenge and exercise in stubbornness. More importantly, it forced me to rethink something I thought I already knew: when does it make sense to build something like this yourself, and when are you better off waiting for the box to show up? My goal with this video is not to talk you out of building a diy tool changer 3d printer (or any open source 3d printer project). I just want to make sure you go into it with the right reasons (and the right expectations), before you blow 2 years and thousands of dollars trying to build something that, at the end of the day, may not outperform something like the Sovol M1D. I DO still think there are plenty of good reasons to build a custom 3d printer or customize something like a voron, a sovol sv08, or a sovol sv08 max - I just think they aren't the reasons you might be expecting. candidates.title: The Genius Illusion Behind Cast Away's Sound
candidates.description: The sound design of Cast Away is one of the film’s greatest hidden achievements. Every sound Tom Hanks makes on the island, including his dialogue, was created from scratch. In this video, we break down how Oscar-winning sound designer Robert Thom rebuilt the entire island through Foley, ADR, Worldizing, wind design, wave recording, and environmental soundscapes to create one of the most invisible feats of sound design in modern cinema. Most fans don’t realize that none of the production sound from the island was usable. Between crashing waves and constant wind, director Robert Zemeckis made the bold decision to rebuild the film’s entire sonic world. That meant every grunt, breath, footstep, creak, wave, and shout (“Wilson!”) had to be designed in post. We explore how Thom and his Foley team sourced unconventional materials like wicker baskets, creaking floors, and twisting wood to simulate palm trees, wind resonance, and environmental tension. We also explore how the film uses water, from gentle fizzing waves to explosive surf impacts, to shape tone and emotional contrast. Then there’s the ADR illusion: the seamless re-recording of Tom Hanks’ dialogue using Walter Murch’s “Worldizing” technique. Hanks recorded clean lines in a studio, then the team blasted them outdoors at Skywalker Ranch to capture realistic distance, echo, and acoustics that matched the empty island. candidates.title: The Colosseum was built on a tyrant's lake
candidates.description: What if the most iconic building in history was actually a political power move? The Colosseum wasn't built for glory. It was built on a tyrant's drained swimming pool, funded by war prisoners, and designed to make one emperor look like a savior. Here's the full story. Nero seized a working-class district after the Great Fire of 64 AD and built himself a private golden palace, complete with his own lake. The people noticed. Rebellion spread, he was declared a public enemy, and he took his own life. Then came Vespasian, and he understood something Nero never did. Power isn't just taken. It's performed. He drained Nero's lake. He built a public arena for 50,000 people on the exact same ground. And he funded the whole thing with war spoils and the labor of prisoners, sending a quiet, unmistakable message to anyone thinking about resisting Rome. When it finally opened, it opened with a hundred days of games. Wild beasts, flooded naval battles, gladiators, and free entry for every Roman citizen. One building. One decade. One of the most effective political campaigns in all of history.

candidates.description: Thomas Cromwell might have pulled off the most meteoric social climb of the 16th century, rising from the son of a blacksmith to become Henry VIII’s chief minister and right hand man. He was a reformer, a champion of the power of Parliament, and the architect of the disillusion of the monasteries. Often seen as a villain of history, his famous depiction in Hillary Mantel’s ‘Wolf Hall’ series presents him in a more sympathetic light. But who was the real Cromwell? How did he rise so high at the Tudor court? And why did he find himself facing execution at the Tower of London? In this episode of the Historic Royal Palaces Podcast, Tracy Borman explores the true history of the man behind the infamy. Joined by Chief Curator Eleri Lynn in the amazing Tudor Great Hall at Hampton Court Palace, she discusses the Reformation, Anne Boleyn, and Cromwell’s all important relationship with Henry VIII. You can find more episodes of the Historic Royal Palaces Podcast wherever you get your podcasts. candidates.description: Take a nostalgic trip through more than two centuries of Independence Day celebrations in the nation's capital! This special explores how Washington, D.C. has honored America's birthday — from Thomas Jefferson's first White House open house in 1801 and John Quincy Adams' impromptu float ride, to the modern-day National Independence Day Parade, the Smithsonian Folklife Festival, A Capitol Fourth concert, and the massive fireworks display over the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. candidates.title: One Performance Makes Zodiac Impossible to Forget
candidates.description: John Carroll Lynch’s Zodiac performance as Arthur Leigh Allen is one of David Fincher’s most unsettling acting showcases. It's an ambiguous, scene-stealing turn in a true crime masterpiece. In this video essay, we break down how John Carroll Lynch makes such a massive impact in Zodiac despite appearing in only a few scenes. As Arthur Leigh Allen, one of the prime suspects in the Zodiac Killer investigation, Lynch creates a performance that feels calm, annoyed, charming, suspicious, and terrifying all at once. David Fincher’s Zodiac is a film built on uncertainty: circumstantial evidence, investigative dead ends, obsession, and the impossible need for closure. Lynch’s portrayal of Arthur Leigh Allen sits right at the center of that ambiguity. Was Allen the Zodiac Killer? Was he an innocent man who happened to look guilty? Or does the brilliance of the performance come from the fact that we can never fully know? We look closely at the famous Zodiac interrogation scene, Fincher’s direction to Lynch, the actor’s preparation, his physical choices, and how the film uses ambiguity to make Allen loom over the entire story. We also discuss Lynch’s career before and after Zodiac, from Fargo to Gothika to American Horror Story, and why this role remains one of his most fascinating performances. This is a John Carroll Lynch acting breakdown, a Zodiac video essay, and a closer look at how one quiet, controlled performance can haunt an entire David Fincher film. 0:00 - I'm not the Zodiac.
